name: vegan spinach ricotta
instructions:
A vegan spinach ricotta from Beth Hornback (Pass the Plants) — variant A is her default recipe as written. Variant B pushes it toward the flavor register of the regular spinach-ricotta-pasta in this cookbook (see sibling note): adds lemon zest/juice, nutmeg, red chili flakes, and porcini mushroom powder to break up the miso/nutritional yeast monotone.

Not the same thing as spinach-ricotta-pasta (which is a proper cooked pasta sauce on real dairy ricotta). This is a raw blended vegan base used as a filling / spread / sauce component.

=== VARIANT A — BETH HORNBACK'S DEFAULT (PASS THE PLANTS) ===

INGREDIENTS:
- 1 cup raw cashews
- 1 (12-oz) package firm or extra-firm tofu, drained (not pressed — moisture helps consistency)
- 2 cups fresh baby spinach (or 1 cup frozen)
- 1/4 cup fresh basil leaves
- 2 cloves garlic
- 1 tsp salt
- 1 tsp light miso paste (white, yellow, or chickpea miso)
- 2 tbsp nutritional yeast

PROCEDURE:
1. In a food processor (see notes on food processor vs blender), pulse the cashews, garlic, MISO, salt, and nutritional yeast until fine and crumbly.
2. Add the tofu, spinach, and basil. Pulse until fully combined — no large tofu or spinach pieces detectable.
3. Use immediately, or refrigerate covered for up to a week (freezes well too).

=== VARIANT B — CLOSER TO THE REGULAR SPINACH RICOTTA PASTA REGISTER (INTENDED FOR PASTA/SPAGHETTI) ===

Variant B is what I've made as a PASTA SAUCE — thin with pasta water and toss with cooked spaghetti or short pasta. Whether the same additions (lemon/nutmeg/chili/porcini) work in a filling application (lasagna, calzones, stuffed shells) is untested — might be good, might not; I don't know yet.

Same method as variant A, plus:
- LEMON ZEST + LEMON JUICE (to taste)
- NUTMEG (a pinch)
- RED CHILI FLAKES (a pinch)
- PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER (small amount — see notes; breaks up the miso/nutritional yeast glutamate monotone)
- DRIED THYME (confirmed successful in the pasta version — added and it helped)

All of these go into the food processor with the tofu/spinach/basil stage. The porcini powder can also go into the initial cashew/miso pulse.

Register-wise this variant reads much closer to the regular spinach-ricotta-pasta in this cookbook (nutmeg + red chili flakes are load-bearing in that recipe; adding them here pulls the vegan version toward that flavor axis).
notes:
Source: Beth Hornback, Pass the Plants blog. Variant A is her recipe as written. Variant B is my extension toward the flavor register of spinach-ricotta-pasta (see sibling note).

=== NO COOK STEP — RAW BLENDED BASE ===

The whole recipe is raw-blended. Nothing cooks. This is a base/filling/spread; the cooking happens downstream when you use it in something baked (lasagna, calzones, stuffed shells, zucchini roll-ups) or tossed with hot pasta. For that reason it's not really a finished dish on its own the way spinach-ricotta-pasta (see below) is.

GENERAL RULE FOR BLENDED-TOFU SAUCES — WARM, DON'T SIMMER: if using this as a pasta sauce, warm it briefly in a pan and toss with hot pasta immediately. Don't try to simmer or reduce a blended-tofu sauce — it doesn't thicken further, doesn't caramelize, and gets grainy if pushed hard. Different from dairy sauces (which benefit from a real reduction step).

=== VARIANT USE CASES — WHAT I'VE ACTUALLY DONE ===

- VARIANT B AS PASTA SAUCE: this is what I've actually made — variant B thinned with pasta water and tossed with cooked spaghetti. Works well.
- VARIANT A AS LASAGNA / CALZONE / STUFFED-SHELL FILLING: this is the intended default use case per Beth's original framing, but I HAVEN'T PERSONALLY TESTED IT YET in something like lasagna. When I try it, log the result here.

=== FOOD PROCESSOR VS BLENDER — FOOD PROCESSOR PROBABLY MORE CORRECT ===

I used a blender for this and it worked, but Beth calls for a food processor and that's probably the more correct choice. Food processor pulses give better control over texture — you can stop at 'coarse' or 'fine crumbly' where the ricotta-like character lands. Blenders tend to over-smooth everything into a paste, which loses some of the texture that makes this read as ricotta-adjacent rather than as a smooth spread.

If using a blender: pulse in short bursts and scrape down often. Don't just leave it on.

=== TOFU CHOICE — SILKEN VS FIRM ===

I USED SILKEN, WHICH MADE A VERY CREAMY SAUCE (GOOD): silken tofu gives a much creamier, more sauce-like final texture than firm tofu. It's good — worth trying if you want the smooth-sauce end of the spectrum.

BUT EITHER IS PROBABLY FINE: Beth's original calls for firm or extra-firm. Firm gives you a chunkier, more ricotta-like final texture that reads closer to the dairy ricotta it's substituting for. Silken pushes toward smooth cream-sauce; firm pushes toward chunky ricotta filling. Pick based on what the downstream dish wants.

CASHEWS MATTER MORE WITH FIRMER TOFU: the cashews add creamy body that the tofu doesn't provide on its own when it's firm. If you're using silken tofu (already creamy), you could probably get away with fewer cashews. With firm/extra-firm, keep the full amount — you need the cashews to bring the sauce together.

=== MISO GOES IN THE BLENDER/PROCESSOR PHASE — DON'T TRY TO FOLD IT IN LATER ===

The miso paste needs to go in during the food-processor phase (with the cashews + garlic + salt + nutritional yeast). Don't try to fold it in during a later skillet phase or off-heat mixing — this is a low-liquid recipe and there's not enough sauce moisture for miso paste to disperse evenly if added late. You'll end up with concentrated miso blobs in an otherwise-bland matrix.

Blender/processor gets the miso distributed properly through the base; later addition doesn't.

=== VARIANT B EXTENSIONS — WHY EACH ADDITION ===

Why the variant B additions:
- LEMON ZEST + JUICE: brightens the whole thing. Zest more important than juice for aroma; juice adds a bit of acid.
- NUTMEG: pairs with dairy-and-cream registers (bechamel, cream sauces). Since this is a dairy-substitute base, the nutmeg lands the same way as it would in actual ricotta.
- RED CHILI FLAKES: background heat and vegetal register — same role they play in the spinach-ricotta-pasta.
- PORCINI MUSHROOM POWDER: this is specifically to break up the miso + nutritional yeast monotone. Miso and nutritional yeast together are the classic 'vegan glutamate bomb' — they cover the same savory-cheesy register from slightly different angles and can read one-note when it's just those two carrying the umami. Porcini adds a different kind of savory depth (woodsy-mushroom) that complements without duplicating. Turns 'flat processed-savory' into 'layered savory.'

=== STORES WELL — FRIDGE + FREEZER ===

Fridge covered up to a week. Freezes well too — worth doubling the batch and freezing half for future lasagna, calzones, or stuffed shells. If doubling, make in TWO batches (too much for a food processor at once, per Beth's note).

=== NOT-CASHEW SUBSTITUTIONS ===

Beth's notes on cashew subs (for nut allergies):
- PEPITAS (raw shelled pumpkin seeds): tested by her, worked well.
- SKIP CASHEWS ENTIRELY + DOUBLE THE TOFU: also works per her; simpler.
Both are valid fallbacks.

=== DRIED HERB ADDITIONS FOR VARIANT B ===

DRIED THYME — CONFIRMED SUCCESSFUL IN THE PASTA VERSION: added thyme to variant B and it helped. Sits with the nutmeg and porcini in the savory-herbaceous register the pasta variant is going for.

WANT TO TRY — HERBES DE PROVENCE AND OREGANO: both untested here but plausible extensions of the herb axis. Herbes de provence would layer with the thyme (already thyme-inclusive as part of that blend) and add sage/lavender/rosemary background. Oregano would push more italian-classical alongside the red chili flakes.

=== SIBLING RECIPES ===

- spinach-ricotta-pasta: the DAIRY version. Real ricotta / food-processed cottage cheese, seared in garlicky oil, folded with cream and food-processor-chopped greens, finished with nutmeg + red chili flakes + lemon. That's a proper cooked pasta sauce; THIS recipe is a raw blended base that gets used inside other dishes. Different dishes, different techniques — not swappable. Variant B here borrows the seasoning register from that recipe but keeps the raw-blended structure.
- lentil-wellington: uses cashews + miso + nutritional yeast in a similar umami stack, but as filling in a savory-baked log rather than as a raw spread. Different application; same underlying vegan-savory principles.
